notes.h: ATP: the energy for muscle contraction
notes.b: Every muscle contraction needs a chemical fuel that the muscle can use immediately. That fuel is ATP, and the body's energy systems exist to keep making more of it.
points: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the only direct source of energy for muscle contraction, so the energy stored in other fuels, such as carbohydrate, fat or phosphocreatine, has to be used to rebuild ATP before the muscle can use it.
Muscles store only enough ATP for about 2 to 3 seconds of work, which means it must be constantly resynthesised (rebuilt) by three energy systems: ATP-PC, lactic acid and aerobic.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the three energy systems. Learn all three names and remember that ATP is the only direct energy source for muscle contraction.

notes.b: The ATP-PC system is the body's fastest way to make ATP. It uses a fuel already stored in the muscle, so it can power short, explosive efforts but runs out quickly.
points: Fuel: phosphocreatine (PC), a chemical stored in the muscle that is used to rebuild ATP. No oxygen is needed, so the system is anaerobic (without oxygen).
Intensity and duration: it is the main supplier for maximal intensity work lasting about 8 to 10 seconds, after which the PC stores are used up.
By-products: none that cause fatigue, which is why it is called alactic (no lactic acid). Fatigue comes from PC running out, not from a waste product building up.
Recovery: PC stores are about half restored in 30 seconds and almost fully restored in about 3 minutes of rest, so a full rest lets a performer repeat a maximal effort.
Sporting examples: 100 m sprint, long jump, shot-put, a tackle, a jump to catch a ball. Each is a very short, all-out effort.
notes.tip: The ATP-PC system does not produce lactic acid. If asked why it causes fatigue, say the PC stores run out. Give times as 'about'.

notes.b: When high-intensity work continues beyond about 10 seconds, PC is running low and the body needs another anaerobic source of ATP. The lactic acid system supplies it by breaking down carbohydrate, but at a price.
points: Fuel: carbohydrate (glycogen, the store of carbohydrate in the muscle, and glucose) broken down without oxygen. This system uses carbohydrate only, not fat.
Intensity and duration: high intensity, from about 10 seconds to about 2 minutes, and it predominates (does most of the work) at roughly 10 to 90 seconds.
By-product: lactic acid (lactate and hydrogen ions), which lowers the pH (makes the muscle more acidic) and so causes fatigue and a burning feeling.
Recovery: removing lactic acid takes much longer than restoring PC, up to about an hour, and is faster with an active cool-down (easy movement after exercise).
Sporting examples: 400 m race, 100 m swim, a long sustained attack in a team game.
notes.tip: Remember that the anaerobic systems use carbohydrate (and PC for ATP-PC) only, while fat is an aerobic fuel. Lactic acid is the cause of fatigue here, so link it to pH and the burning feeling.

notes.b: For anything longer than about 2 minutes, the body relies on oxygen. The aerobic system is slower to deliver ATP, but it can keep going for hours and does not cause fatigue.
points: Fuel: carbohydrate and fat (protein only in extreme cases), broken down with oxygen. Using fat as well as carbohydrate is what lets the system last so long.
Intensity and duration: low to moderate intensity, from about 2 minutes to several hours, and it predominates beyond about 2 minutes.
By-products: carbon dioxide and water, which are easily removed (the body breathes out the carbon dioxide), so there are no fatigue-causing by-products.
It produces far more ATP from each molecule of fuel than the anaerobic systems, but more slowly, so it cannot supply the quick bursts of ATP that sprints need.
Sporting examples: marathon, 10 km open-water swim, the background work of a Gaelic football match.
It also powers recovery between high-intensity efforts, such as restoring PC between sprints, because the aerobic system supplies the ATP the body needs to rebuild its PC stores.
notes.tip: If asked why an activity uses the aerobic system, give its duration and its low to moderate intensity. Don't forget that the aerobic system uses fat as well as carbohydrate.

notes.h: The energy continuum and relative contribution
notes.b: The three systems are not separate switches. They work together as a continuum (a smooth scale), and what changes with the activity is which one does most of the work.
points: All three systems work at all times; the one that predominates depends on the duration and intensity of the activity. Do not say a system 'switches on' only after another runs out.

Short, maximal activities rely mainly on ATP-PC; high-intensity efforts lasting up to about 2 minutes rely mainly on the lactic acid system; longer, moderate efforts rely mainly on the aerobic system.
Main system by event: long jump (3 to 5 seconds, high intensity) ATP-PC; 400 m (45 seconds or more, high intensity) lactic acid; marathon (2 hours or more, low to medium intensity) aerobic.

Intermittent team games (bursts of effort with rests) use all three: ATP-PC for sprints, jumps and tackles; lactic acid for repeated efforts with short recovery; aerobic for the overall duration and for recovery between efforts.

On an energy-system graph of contribution against time, the ATP-PC line peaks first and falls within about 10 seconds, the lactic acid line peaks next, and the aerobic line rises steadily and dominates after about 2 minutes.
notes.tip: To pick the main system, match the event's duration and intensity (marathon aerobic, 400 m lactic acid, long jump ATP-PC). On a graph, identify the aerobic line as the one that rises steadily and dominates later. For a team game, describe how two systems contribute.

notes.h: Using the energy systems in preparation, performance and recovery
notes.b: Knowing which system an activity relies on lets athletes and coaches plan smarter. The same knowledge guides how to train, how to compete and how to recover.
points: Preparation: train the predominant system (specificity, meaning training matches the demands of the activity). For ATP-PC, use short maximal sprints with full recovery; for the lactic acid system, repeated high-intensity intervals with short recovery to build tolerance of lactic acid; for the aerobic system, continuous or long-interval training.
Work-to-rest ratios match the system: for ATP-PC, about 1:3 or longer so PC is restored before the next effort; for the lactic acid system, shorter recovery; aerobic work is near-continuous.
Performance: pacing strategy matters, because going too hard early in a 400 m or 1500 m race floods the muscles with lactic acid and causes early fatigue.
Performance: substitutions and breaks in play (tactical rests) let team players restore PC between efforts.
Recovery: an active cool-down removes lactic acid faster; carbohydrate refuels glycogen for the lactic acid and aerobic systems; full rest between maximal efforts restores PC.
Diet link: carbohydrate fuels the lactic acid and aerobic systems; creatine supplementation aims to raise PC stores for the ATP-PC system.
notes.tip: When asked how energy-system knowledge informs training, link each system to a specific session type and its work-to-rest ratio, rather than just saying 'train the system'.

notes.b: Two swimming events at opposite ends of the continuum show how the same knowledge is applied. One is a short, intense race and the other a very long, steady one.
points: 100 m backstroke: about one minute at very high intensity, so the ATP-PC system powers the start and the lactic acid system supplies most of the race.
Preparation for the 100 m backstroke focuses on maximal starts and turns with full recovery (to restore PC) and on high-intensity intervals with short recovery (to build tolerance of lactic acid).
10 km open-water swim: about two hours at moderate intensity, so the aerobic system supplies almost all the energy, using carbohydrate and fat.
Preparation for the 10 km swim focuses on long continuous swims and long intervals, pacing practice and feeding with carbohydrate during the race to keep fuel available.
notes.tip: For two contrasting events, name the main system for each, give the reason from duration and intensity, then link each system to a different type of preparation. Use these reasoning steps rather than any times or swimmers from a past paper.

keyTerms.definition: Adenosine triphosphate, the only direct source of energy for muscle contraction.
A high-energy compound stored in muscle that rapidly resynthesises ATP in the ATP-PC system.
The anaerobic system that uses phosphocreatine for maximal efforts of about 8 to 10 seconds, with no fatiguing by-products.
The anaerobic system that breaks down carbohydrate without oxygen for high-intensity efforts of about 10 seconds to 2 minutes, producing lactic acid.
The system that breaks down carbohydrate and fat with oxygen for low to moderate intensity over long durations, producing carbon dioxide and water.
A by-product of the lactic acid system that lowers muscle pH and causes fatigue.
The idea that all three energy systems always contribute, with the predominant one set by the duration and intensity of the activity.

factCards.term: Main energy system: marathon, 400 m, long jump
factCards.definition: Marathon: aerobic. 400 m: lactic acid. Long jump: ATP-PC.

factCards.term: How long PC takes to restore
factCards.definition: About half in 30 seconds; almost fully in about 3 minutes.
ATP-PC: none that cause fatigue. Lactic acid: lactic acid. Aerobic: carbon dioxide and water.

questions.prompt: Explain how an understanding of the ATP-PC and aerobic energy systems can inform preparation for a sprint event and an endurance event.
questions.model: The ATP-PC system uses stored phosphocreatine without oxygen to supply energy for maximal efforts of about 8 to 10 seconds, with no fatiguing by-products; PC is almost fully restored after about 3 minutes' rest. For a 100 m sprinter, training should be short, maximal sprints and starts with long recovery (about 1:3 or more), so each effort is at full intensity on full PC stores, plus strength and power work. The aerobic system uses carbohydrate and fat with oxygen at low to moderate intensity for long durations, producing carbon dioxide and water. For a marathon runner, training should be long continuous runs and long intervals in the aerobic zone to improve oxygen delivery and use, with high-carbohydrate meals and carbohydrate loading before the race and carbohydrate during it, because glycogen depletion causes fatigue. Recovery also differs: the sprinter needs full rest between efforts, while the endurance athlete needs glycogen refuelling and rehydration.

questions.prompt: Describe how two energy systems contribute to performance in a team game of your choice.
questions.model: Game: soccer. The ATP-PC system supplies energy for short, maximal actions lasting up to about 10 seconds, such as a sprint to beat a defender, a jump to head the ball or a shot, using stored phosphocreatine without oxygen. The aerobic system supplies energy for the 90 minutes of jogging, running and positioning, using carbohydrate and fat with oxygen, and also restores PC between sprints, so a player with good aerobic fitness recovers faster and can repeat high-intensity efforts late in the game.

questions.prompt: Identify the main energy system for a marathon, a 400 m race and a long jump, and give a reason for each.
questions.model: Marathon: aerobic, because it lasts over two hours at low to moderate intensity. 400 m: lactic acid system, because it is a high-intensity effort lasting about 45 seconds or more. Long jump: ATP-PC, because the run-up and take-off are a maximal effort lasting only a few seconds.
